lessons.title: Determining Harvest Maturity
lessons.body:
Harvest bananas at the right stage to get good taste, long shelf life, and top market price. For local markets, harvest when fruits are mature but still green, with no yellow. For export, harvest even earlier, when fingers are fully formed but before any ripening starts. In Africa, most bananas are harvested by checking the age of the bunch. From flowering to harvest, typical times are: 80â90 days for sweet bananas (like Sukari), 90â100 days for cooking bananas (like Matoke), and 100â120 days for plantains. Mark the flowering date on a stick or record it in a notebook. When that number of days is reached, start checking.

Look at the fruit. Mature green bananas have rounded fingers with no sharp angles. The tips of the fingers lose their dark colour and become lighter green. The bunch stalk (peduncle) starts to turn from green to light yellow-green. Cut a test finger from the middle of the bunch and slice it across. The seeds should be small and black, and the flesh should be firm, not watery. If you see white sap, it's still too early. For export, the fruit must be at 75â80% maturity, meaning the fingers are full but not ripe. A simple tool is a maturity chart with colour photos, available from extension officers.

Do not harvest too early: fruits will shrivel and never ripen well. Do not harvest too late: fruits ripen on the tree, split, and attract insects. In hot areas, maturity comes faster; in cool highlands, slower. Adjust days by 5â10 days based on altitude. For best results, harvest in the cool morning hours. If you sell to a processor, ask them for their preferred maturity stage. Always test a few bunches before harvesting the whole field.

lessons.title: Harvesting Techniques and Tools
lessons.body:
Harvest bananas carefully to avoid bruises that reduce price. Use the right tools: a sharp curved knife or machete for cutting the bunch, and a forked pole (made from a strong stick with a V-shape at the top) to support the bunch as you cut. For tall plants, a ladder or climbing harness helps. Never pull the bunch down by handâit damages the crown and fingers.

First, clear the area around the plant. Cut the bunch stalk about 30â45 cm above the first hand. With one person supporting the bunch with the forked pole, another cuts the stalk with a clean, sharp knife. Lower the bunch gently to the ground or onto a clean tarp or banana leaves. Do not drop it. For export bananas, cut the bunch with a long stalk (about 15â20 cm) and leave the bunch whole until you reach the packing shed.

After cutting, immediately place the bunch in the shade. If you leave it in the sun, the fruit heats up and ripens too fast. Use a wheelbarrow or a small cart with padding to move bunches to the collection point. Do not stack more than two bunches high. For plantains and cooking bananas, you can harvest the whole bunch and hang it in a cool shed.

Clean your tools with soap and water or a 10% bleach solution between plants to prevent spreading diseases like banana bunchy top virus. Wear gloves to protect your hands from sap, which stains and irritates. In dry areas, harvest early in the morning or late evening. In wet areas, avoid harvesting during rain to reduce fungal growth. Always harvest with a partner for safety and efficiency.

lessons.title: Dehanding and Cluster Preparation
lessons.body:
Dehanding means separating the bunch into individual hands or smaller clusters. This is done in a shaded area, preferably on a clean table or mat. For local markets, many farmers sell whole bunches, but for higher prices, dehand and sell hands or clusters. For export, dehanding is done in a packing shed with running water and clean knives.

To dehand, hold the bunch by the stalk. Use a sharp, clean knife to cut between the hands, leaving a small piece of the crown (the cushion) attached to each hand. Do not cut into the fingers. For clusters, cut hands into groups of 3â6 fingers. This is popular for supermarkets and hotels. For plantains, you can leave hands whole or cut into smaller pieces for cooking. Always cut on a plastic or stainless steel surface, not on bare ground, to avoid contamination.

After dehanding, trim the fingers: remove any damaged, bruised, or undersized fingers. Also trim the flower remnants (the black tip) with a small knife or scissors. Be careful not to cut the skin of neighbouring fingers. For export, leave the crown intact and trim the fingers to a uniform length. For local markets, you can leave the natural crown but remove any dried flower parts.

Work quickly and keep the fruit in the shade. Sap from the cut crown can stain the fruit; wipe it off with a clean cloth. Do not wash the fruit yet if you are not going to pack immediately. Place dehanded clusters in clean plastic crates lined with banana leaves or newspaper. Do not pile more than three layers high. Keep the crates in a cool, shaded area until packaging. This step adds value and reduces waste.

lessons.title: Cleaning, Grading, and Sorting
lessons.body:
Cleaning removes dirt, sap, and insects. For local markets, wipe each finger with a dry or slightly damp clean cloth. For export, wash the fruit in clean water with a small amount of food-grade detergent (2 ml per litre) and then rinse with clean water. Do not soak the fruit; dip quickly and shake off excess water. Use a soft brush for stubborn dirt. After washing, dry the fruit with a clean cloth or air-dry in the shade. Never use dirty waterâit spreads disease.

Grading means sorting fruit by size, shape, and colour. For export, bananas are graded by finger length and diameter. Common grades: Extra Class (perfect, no defects), Class I (minor defects), Class II (more defects but still good). For local markets, grade into: Grade A (large, clean, no spots), Grade B (small or slight spots), and Grade C (damaged, for processing). Use a sizing ring or a simple ruler to measure finger diameter. For export, fingers should be 12â14 cm long and 3.2â3.8 cm in diameter for standard Cavendish. For local, any size is acceptable but uniform size sells better.

Sorting also removes any fruit with signs of disease, insect damage, or over-ripeness. These should be sold quickly or processed into flour, chips, or animal feed. Keep different grades separate in different crates. Label each crate with the grade and date. For export, follow the buyer's specific grade standards. In Africa, many cooperatives have grading tables with pictures. Ask your extension officer for a copy.

After grading, pack immediately or store in a cool room (13â15Â°C) for up to 24 hours. Do not store near ethylene-producing fruits like mangoes or tomatoes. Clean your hands and tools between grades to avoid mixing. Good grading gets you better prices and repeat customers.

lessons.title: Packaging for Local and Export Markets
lessons.body:
Packaging protects bananas from bruising, dirt, and moisture loss. For local markets, use clean plastic crates (60x40x30 cm) lined with banana leaves or newspaper. Do not use sacksâthey crush the fruit. For short transport, you can use baskets lined with cloth. For export, use standard corrugated cardboard boxes with ventilation holes. The box size is usually 50x30x25 cm and holds about 18â20 kg of bananas. Line the box with a perforated polyethylene liner (0.04 mm thick) to keep humidity high. Place a paper towel or absorbent pad at the bottom to soak up sap.

Pack bananas in clusters or hands, not single fingers, for export. Arrange them in the box in a single layer, with crowns facing down or to the side. Do not overfill; leave 2â3 cm of space at the top. For local markets, you can pack hands or whole bunches in crates, but keep them loose. For plantains, pack in crates with leaves between layers. Always label the box with: product name, grade, count (number of fingers or hands), weight, origin, and date. For export, include the farm code and traceability number.

Use cushioning material like shredded paper or foam nets for premium markets. Avoid using newspaper with coloured ink directly touching the fruit. For organic markets, use compostable liners and boxes. In Africa, many exporters use reusable plastic crates (foldable) to reduce cost. After packing, stack boxes no more than 5 high for cardboard, 8 high for plastic crates. Keep out of direct sun and rain. For air freight, pack in smaller boxes (10 kg) to meet airline rules. Always check with your buyer for specific packaging requirements before harvest.

lessons.title: Transportation and Cold Chain Management
lessons.body:
Bananas are sensitive to heat, cold, and vibration. After harvest, the goal is to cool them quickly and keep them cool until they reach the buyer. For local markets, transport in the early morning or evening when it's cool. Use a covered vehicle or cover the crates with a tarpaulin. Do not transport in open trucks under hot sun. For short distances (under 2 hours), you can use a bicycle or motorcycle with a padded box. For longer distances, use a truck with good suspension. Stack crates securely to prevent movement.

For export or long-distance transport, you need a cold chain. Pre-cool the bananas to 13â15Â°C within 24 hours of harvest. Use a forced-air cooler or a cold room. Then load into a refrigerated truck or container set at 13â15Â°C. Do not go below 12Â°Câchilling injury causes black spots and failure to ripen. Keep relative humidity at 90â95%. Use a data logger to record temperature during transit. If you don't have a cold room, use a well-insulated truck with ice packs for short trips, but this is only for local high-value markets.

For air freight, pack in insulated boxes with gel packs. Keep the boxes in a cool area at the airport. For sea freight, use a controlled atmosphere container with 2â5% oxygen and 2â5% carbon dioxide to slow ripening. This allows 20â30 days of transport. Always pre-cool before loading. In Africa, many exporters use refrigerated containers at the port. Work with a freight forwarder who understands perishables.

At the destination, unload quickly into a cool area. Do not break the cold chain. For local markets, sell within 2â3 days. For export, the buyer will ripen the bananas in special rooms. Keep records of temperatures and times. Good cold chain management reduces losses from 30% to under 5%.

quiz.q: What is the typical time from flowering to harvest for sweet bananas like Sukari?
quiz.explanation: Sweet bananas typically take 80â90 days from flowering to harvest.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to support the bunch while cutting it from the plant?
quiz.explanation: A forked pole supports the bunch to prevent it from falling and bruising.

quiz.q: What is the recommended concentration of bleach solution for cleaning tools between plants?
quiz.explanation: A 10% bleach solution is effective for disinfecting tools to prevent disease spread.

quiz.q: What does 'dehanding' mean?
options: A) Removing the flower from the banana
B) Separating the bunch into individual hands or clusters
quiz.explanation: Dehanding is the process of separating the bunch into hands or smaller clusters.

quiz.q: For export, what is the ideal finger diameter for standard Cavendish bananas?
quiz.explanation: Export-grade Cavendish bananas typically have a finger diameter of 3.2â3.8 cm.

quiz.q: Why should you not harvest bananas during rain?
options: A) The fruit will be too wet to sell
B) It increases the risk of fungal growth
D) The sap will wash away
quiz.explanation: Harvesting in rain increases moisture and the risk of fungal diseases on the fruit.

quiz.q: What is the recommended storage temperature for bananas before packaging?
quiz.explanation: Bananas should be stored at 13â15Â°C to slow ripening without causing chilling injury.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of maturity in green bananas?
options: B) Rounded fingers with no sharp angles
quiz.explanation: Mature green bananas have rounded fingers and lose their sharp angles.

quiz.q: What should you do immediately after cutting a banana bunch?
options: A) Leave it in the sun to dry
B) Place it in the shade
quiz.explanation: Placing the bunch in the shade prevents heat buildup and slows ripening.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a perforated polyethylene liner in an export box?
options: A) To keep the fruit cool
quiz.explanation: The liner helps maintain high humidity around the fruit, reducing moisture loss.

quiz.q: Which grade of bananas is typically used for processing?
quiz.explanation: Grade C bananas are damaged or over-ripe and are suitable for processing.

quiz.q: What is the first step in cleaning bananas for export?
options: A) Soak in detergent for 10 minutes
B) Wipe with a dry cloth
C) Dip in clean water with food-grade detergent
D) Scrub with a hard brush
quiz.explanation: For export, bananas are quickly dipped in water with a small amount of food-grade detergent.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid stacking more than two bunches high during harvest?
quiz.explanation: Stacking too high causes pressure and bruising on the lower bunches.

quiz.q: What is the ideal relative humidity for banana storage?
quiz.explanation: High humidity of 90â95% prevents moisture loss and shriveling.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a recommended packaging material for local markets?
quiz.explanation: Sacks crush the fruit and are not recommended for packaging bananas.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of transporting bananas in an open truck under hot sun?
options: B) Rapid ripening and heat damage
quiz.explanation: Exposure to sun causes heat buildup, leading to rapid ripening and damage.

quiz.q: What does a data logger do in cold chain management?
quiz.explanation: A data logger records temperature to ensure the cold chain is maintained.

quiz.q: For sea freight, what controlled atmosphere is used to slow ripening?
quiz.explanation: Controlled atmosphere with 2â5% O2 and 2â5% CO2 slows ripening during sea transport.

quiz.q: What is the recommended temperature for a refrigerated container for bananas?
quiz.explanation: Bananas should be transported at 13â15Â°C to avoid chilling injury.

quiz.q: Why should you not store bananas near mangoes or tomatoes?
options: B) They produce ethylene that speeds ripening
quiz.explanation: Mangoes and tomatoes produce ethylene gas, which accelerates banana ripening.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of trimming the flower remnants after dehanding?
quiz.explanation: Trimming flower remnants improves the appearance and marketability of the fruit.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common maturity test for bananas?
options: B) Cutting a finger and checking seed colour
quiz.explanation: Cutting a finger and checking for small black seeds indicates maturity.

quiz.q: What is the maximum stack height for cardboard boxes of bananas?
quiz.explanation: Cardboard boxes should not be stacked more than 5 high to prevent crushing.

quiz.q: What is the first step in grading bananas?
options: B) Sorting by size and colour
quiz.explanation: Grading starts with sorting fruit by size, shape, and colour.

quiz.q: Why is it important to clean tools between plants?
options: D) To make them last longer
quiz.explanation: Cleaning tools prevents the spread of diseases like bunchy top virus.

quiz.q: What is the ideal time of day for harvesting bananas?
options: B) Early morning or late evening
quiz.explanation: Harvesting in cooler parts of the day reduces heat stress on the fruit.

quiz.q: What is a common cushioning material for premium banana packaging?
quiz.explanation: Shredded paper or foam nets are used to cushion fruit in premium packs.

quiz.q: What is the recommended pre-cooling temperature for bananas before transport?
quiz.explanation: Pre-cooling to 13â15Â°C removes field heat and prepares for cold chain.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a grade for export bananas?
quiz.explanation: Export grades are Extra Class, Class I, and Class II; Grade D is not standard.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of good cold chain management?
options: B) Reduces losses from 30% to under 5%
quiz.explanation: Proper cold chain reduces post-harvest losses significantly.
